transcription.tex: \textbf{The modulus of a number}\par The modulus of \(a\), written \(\lvert a\rvert\), is its non-negative numerical value.\[\lvert6\rvert=6,\qquad\lvert-7.1\rvert=7.1.\]\[\lvert a\rvert=\begin{cases}a,&a\ge0,\\-a,&a<0.\end{cases}\]

\textbf{Distance and magnitude}\par The distance between two numbers \(a\) and \(b\) is \(\lvert b-a\rvert\), regardless of their order.\par For example, the distance between 2 and 7 is\[\lvert7-2\rvert=\lvert2-7\rvert=5.\]\par Modulus measures size: distances and speeds are non-negative. The same notation \(\lvert\mathbf a\rvert\) gives the magnitude (length) of a vector.

\textbf{How to sketch \(y=\lvert ax+b\rvert\)}\par Sketch \(y=ax+b\). Keep the part on or above the \(x\)-axis and reflect the part below the axis upwards.\par Every output of a modulus function is non-negative.

transcription.tex: The dotted line is \(y=2x-3\). Reflect its negative part upwards. The vertex is \((\tfrac32,0)\).
\[\begin{aligned}2x-3&=5\Rightarrow x=4,\\3-2x&=5\Rightarrow x=-1.\end{aligned}\]\par Both values are valid.
The modulus graph lies above the line outside the intersections:\[x<\frac65\quad\text{or}\quad x>2.\]\par Strict inequality excludes both endpoints.

transcription.tex: \textbf{1.} Solve \(\lvert x+1\rvert=2x+5\). There is only one solution.
For \(x\ge-1\), \(x+1=2x+5\) gives \(x=-4\), outside this branch, so reject it.\par For \(x<-1\):\[-x-1=2x+5\Rightarrow x=-2.\]\par Check: \(\lvert-2+1\rvert=1=2(-2)+5\).

The boundary equations are\[\begin{aligned}4x-1&=2x\Rightarrow x=\tfrac12,\\1-4x&=2x\Rightarrow x=\tfrac16.\end{aligned}\]\par The blue graph is below the red line between the intersections:\[\frac16<x<\frac12.\]

\[\begin{aligned}4-\tfrac32x&=5\Rightarrow x=-\tfrac23,\\\tfrac32x-4&=5\Rightarrow x=6.\end{aligned}\]\par The vertex is \((\tfrac83,0)\); the vertical intercept is 4.

There are no intersections, so no solutions.\par For \(x\le6\), the equation gives \(x=\tfrac{22}3>6\), outside that branch.\par For \(x\ge6\), it gives \(x=2<6\), again outside the branch.

\textbf{13.} The equation \(\lvert6-x\rvert=\tfrac12x+k\) has exactly one solution.\par (a) Find \(k\). (2 marks)\par (b) State the solution. (2 marks)
Exactly one intersection occurs at the vertex \((6,0)\):\[0=\tfrac12(6)+k\Rightarrow k=-3.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{What is a mapping?}\par A mapping relates a set of inputs to a set of outputs. It may follow a rule or be described by individual arrows.\par The \textbf{domain} is the set of possible inputs. The \textbf{range} is the set of outputs that are actually reached.

\textbf{An arbitrary mapping}\[0\mapsto4.4\text{ and }7.2,\qquad2\mapsto1,\qquad3.1\mapsto7.2.\]\par One input can relate to several outputs; different inputs can share an output. Some listed inputs may have no arrow.

\textbf{Example: \(x\mapsto2x\)}\[\begin{array}{c|rrrr}x&-1&0&1.7&2\\\hline2x&-2&0&3.4&4\end{array}\]\par A general relation may have more than one output for an input, or no output for some listed inputs. A function has a stricter rule, explored next.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{A function maps every element of its domain to exactly one output.}\par Notation: \(f(x)=2x+1\) or \(f:x\mapsto2x+1\). Here \(f(x)\) denotes the output for input \(x\).\par A graph represents the points \((x,f(x))\). The vertical line test checks whether an input has more than one output.
Every vertical line meets the graph at most once.
A positive input gives two outputs.
Every real input has exactly one real output.
Negative inputs have no real output, so this domain is not valid.
For example, input 4 gives both 2 and \(-2\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: Each input of a function has one output. Different inputs may still share the same output. The horizontal line test distinguishes these two types.
\textbf{One-to-one}\par Every output in the range comes from exactly one input.\par Example: \(f(x)=2x+1\).
\(2\mapsto5,\quad3\mapsto7,\quad4\mapsto9\).\par No horizontal line intersects the graph more than once.
\textbf{Many-to-one}\par Two or more inputs can have the same output.\par Example: \(f(x)=x^2\), \(x\in\mathbb R\).
\(f(2)=4\) and \(f(-2)=4\).\par The horizontal line \(y=4\) intersects twice.

transcription.tex: A \textbf{piecewise function} uses different rules on different parts of its domain.\[f(x)=\begin{cases}5-2x,&x<1,\\x^2+3,&x\ge1.\end{cases}\]\par (a) Sketch \(y=f(x)\) and state the range.\par (b) Solve \(f(x)=19\).
The left branch approaches 3 but does not reach it. The right branch starts at 4. Together they give\[f(x)>3.\]\par An open circle excludes an endpoint; a filled circle includes it.

For \(x<1\): \(5-2x=19\Rightarrow x=-7\).\par For \(x\ge1\): \(x^2+3=19\Rightarrow x=\pm4\). Only \(x=4\) is in this branch.\par Therefore \(x=-7\) or \(x=4\).\par Reject \(x=-4\): it belongs to the unused part of the quadratic.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C4 June 2012, Q6(a)}\par \(f(x)=e^x+2\), \(x\in\mathbb R\). State the range of \(f\).
Since \(e^x>0\), the range is \(f(x)>2\).\par The asymptote \(y=2\) is never reached.
\textbf{Edexcel C4 June 2010, Q4(d)}\par \(g(x)=x^2-4x+1\), \(0\le x\le5\). Find the range.
\(g(x)=(x-2)^2-3\), so the minimum is \(-3\) at \(x=2\).\par At the domain endpoints, \(g(0)=1\) and \(g(5)=6\).\par Hence \(-3\le g(x)\le6\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{7.} The function \(s\) is defined by\[s(x)=\begin{cases}x^2-6,&x<0,\\10-x,&x\ge0.\end{cases}\]\par (a) Sketch \(y=s(x)\).\par (b) Find all \(a\) such that \(s(a)=43\).\par (c) Solve \(s(x)=x\).
For \(a<0\): \(a^2-6=43\Rightarrow a=\pm7\); retain \(a=-7\).\par For \(a\ge0\): \(10-a=43\Rightarrow a=-33\), outside this branch.\par The only solution is \(a=-7\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{8.} The function \(p\) is defined by\[p(x)=\begin{cases}e^{-x},&-5\le x<0,\\x^3+4,&0\le x\le4.\end{cases}\]\par (a) Sketch \(y=p(x)\).\par (b) Find all \(a\), to 2 decimal places, such that \(p(a)=50\).
The left branch ends at the open point \((0,1)\); the right branch starts at the filled point \((0,4)\).

On the negative branch:\[e^{-a}=50\Rightarrow-a=\ln50\Rightarrow a=-3.91.\]\par On the non-negative branch:\[a^3+4=50\Rightarrow a=\sqrt[3]{46}=3.58.\]\par Both values lie within their branch domains.\par The solutions are \(a=-3.91\) and \(a=3.58\), to 2 decimal places.

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{9.} The function \(h\) has domain \(-10\le x\le6\). It is linear from \((-10,14)\) to \((-4,2)\), and from \((-4,2)\) to \((6,27)\).\par (a) Sketch \(y=h(x)\).\par (b) State the range.\par (c) Find all \(a\) such that \(h(a)=12\).
The lowest output is 2 and the greatest is 27.\[2\le h(x)\le27.\]

The first segment has slope \(-2\), so \(h(x)=-2x-6\).\[-2a-6=12\Rightarrow a=-9.\]\par The second has slope \(\tfrac52\), so \(h(x)=\tfrac52x+12\).\[\tfrac52a+12=12\Rightarrow a=0.\]\par Both lie in the corresponding intervals.

transcription.tex: \textbf{11.} \(f(x)=ax^3+bx-5\), where \(a,b\) are constants. Given \(f(1)=-4\) and \(f(2)=9\), find \(a,b\).
\textbf{12.} \(h(x)=x^2-6x+20\), with domain \(x\ge a\). Given that \(h\) is one-to-one, find the smallest possible \(a\). (6 marks)

\[h(x)=(x-3)^2+11.\]\par The vertex is \((3,11)\). The function is one-to-one on the increasing branch \(x\ge3\). Any smaller lower bound includes two inputs with the same output.\par Therefore the smallest possible value is \(a=3\).
